then.text: Our Firth pilot! Crossing again? The Firth's not changed its mind about anything, so hold on.
You did WHAT on Duncansby shore? Faced the Nuckelavee and lived to tell me about it on my own quay? Well. That's a story for the bar for twenty years.

Here. Fresh water from the burn above the town, corked and blessed by nobody in particular. The old folk say the Nuckelavee can't abide fresh water. Keep it handy. And this badge says you've crossed the Firth and come home. Not everybody does both.
Now. Orkney? We sail when you're ready.
Remember: the Tide Watcher at the Merry Men of Mey for the tables, then the tables to my opposite number on the Kirkwall quay. Ready to sail?

else.text: Orkney, is it? The Pentland Firth is no millpond. The tides race through at some of the fastest speeds round Britain, the Atlantic meets the North Sea, and the two of them argue all day.

I'll make you a deal. My tide tables blew overboard, which is embarrassing for a skipper. The Tide Watcher at the Merry Men of Mey, east along the coast, keeps her own. Win her respect and her copy, take it to my mate on the Kirkwall quay, and you'll have crossed the Firth like a pilot, not a passenger.
Or just sail now and do it the other way about. The Firth doesn't mind who goes first.

rail_guard.text: Thurso. The most northerly station in Britain, and the end of the line, which round here is a compliment. Four hours to Inverness across the Flow Country. Bring a piece.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited in Great Britain. Where to?

flagstone_mason.text: See these fences? Caithness flags, stood up on end in a row, each one a slab of stone near a man's height. No mortar. No posts. They've stood through gales for two hundred years.
The stone is Old Red Sandstone, laid down in a huge lake about three hundred and eighty million years ago. It splits as flat as a table. Thurso's pavements, roofs, floors, byres, the lot.
There's a flagstone trail at Castletown, along the road east, where the quarries were. They say Caithness flags paved half the cities of the Empire. I say: the good half.

then.text: The bus to Wick got cancelled 'cause of wind. The bus is fine. The bus has been through worse. The bus is a coward.

else.text: Nothing ever happens here. Except surfing. And the Northern Lights. And orcas in the Firth. And the ferry. Fine. Some things happen.
Did you know it's light till nearly midnight in June? You can play footie at eleven at night. Nobody's mum believes that's a reason to stay out.

nc500_tourist.text: The North Coast 500! Five hundred-odd miles round the top of Scotland, starting and finishing at Inverness. We've done the Bealach na Bà, Durness, Smoo Cave and four thousand passing places.
Smoo Cave is incredible: one of the biggest sea cave entrances in Britain, with a waterfall inside. My husband says the waterfall was the best bit. He also says that about every lay-by.

flow_runner.text: Training for a run across the Flow Country. On the road, mind. Nobody runs across a bog twice.
Fun fact: blanket bog covers about a fifth of Caithness and Sutherland. Not-fun fact: so do the clegs. Horseflies. They bite through Lycra.

landsky_stacks.text: {greeting} I count fulmars on the stacks along the coast. The sea does the sculpture, I do the sums.

A headland goes like this. Waves find a crack and hammer it into a cave. The cave breaks through and you've an arch. The arch falls and leaves a pillar: a stack. The stack wears down to a stump at low tide, and the sea starts on the next headland. Takes a few thousand years, or one bad winter.

Caithness is flagstone, mud from the floor of a huge lake nearly 400 million years ago, and it splits in sheets. The Duncansby stacks along the coast are it, and the Old Man of Hoy over the water is the same Old Red Sandstone. Fulmars nest on the ledges and spit at you. I count them anyway.

then.text: Nets full and the water quiet. The biologist says the quiet's the trouble. I'm choosing not to hear her.
Auld Willie's gone off in somebody's team, and the nets are full. I keep looking at the rock. It feels wrong to be glad.

else.text: New nets, tighter, heavier, and a hoop on the end. Willie tries them every month. They hold.

ct_seal_willie.text: Willie's still on his rock at the river mouth. The fish are still scarce. Hamish has stopped shouting at him, which I take as the first honest thing anybody's said about it.
